E0314.summary: Degrees of concentration through which, Atwood says, the agent is promoted and fortified; she does not explain them further.
E0314.body: Atwood speaks of the agent being fortified “when promoted through a second to a third of concentration” [III.4 ¶9]. The text names these degrees but does not explain what each involves.

E0315.summary: The receiving medium through which universal principles are conceived; Atwood says nature lacks a true one, and that truth depends on its purity.
E0315.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood says: “There is no such thing as truth absolute in nature, because she has no true conceptive vehicle” [APP ¶43]. The receiving medium must be pure and simple if truth is to be conceived: “Thus everything depends on the purity of the receiving power.” [APP ¶43]. See also *conceptive vehicle*.

E0316.summary: The vehicle of conception; Atwood blames the ancients' obscure teaching about it for great error, and says the soul may dissolve its own, the parental bond.
E0316.body: Atwood says that “the obscure instructions of the ancients concerning the nature of their conceptive vehicle, has caused incalculable error and confusion” [II.1 ¶8]; she does not define it further there. Elsewhere she treats it as the soul's vehicle from conception, which the soul may dissolve, and identifies it with the parental bond: “she may dissolve her own conceptive vehicle, even the parental bond” [II.3 ¶37]. In the Appendix (a later layer) she says nature “has no true conceptive vehicle” [APP ¶43]; see *conceptive medium*.

E0317.summary: In Norton's verses, an agreement or fit between the art and its requisites, numbered as successive Concords (ministers, places, instrument).
E0317.body: The term comes chiefly from Norton, quoted by Atwood. He numbers the Concords: “The Second Concord with this Arte is,” [III.4 ¶36] (concerning apt ministers), and “The Fourth Concord is full notable Between this arte and places convenable” [III.4 ¶41]. He also speaks of the fit of the art with its instrument: “Without full concord of arte with hys instrument” [III.4 ¶39]. Atwood herself uses ‘concord’ for the joining of prayer, self-sacrifice and the faculties of the mind [III.4 ¶28].

E0318.summary: Cited once, critically: Atwood rejects his sensual system, together with Locke's.
E0318.body: Atwood names Condillac only to criticize his sensual system, along with Locke's [II.1 ¶34].

E0319.summary: What man can do in the work: prepare the conditions by patient, disciplined labour, without being able to compel the Divine blessing.
E0319.body: Atwood: “Man may conditionate: --- ought, by patient labour disciplining, to prepare the way of the Greater in the Lesser Good” [III.4 ¶20]. The context sets this human preparation against the Divine blessing, which man cannot compel. See *conditionating*.

E0320.summary: Placing oneself under conditions in obedience to the Divine Will, as opposed to searching in one's own will alone.
E0320.body: Atwood contrasts searching in one's own will alone with proceeding “by conditionating, in obedience to the Divine Will” [IV.4 ¶23]. See *conditionate*.

E0321.summary: The mixture or compound of the work; Hermes says the ferment whitens it, and Atwood warns that a premature permanent confection yields an offspring that does not abide.
E0321.body: Hermes, quoted by Atwood, says “the ferment whitens the confection” [I.3 ¶58], and protects it from combustion. Atwood uses the word for a permanent fixing that must not come too early: “if any permanent confection is made or suffered to take place beforehand, the immature offspring does not abide” [IV.1 ¶48].

E0322.summary: A fitting faculty of sight without which, Atwood says, the research cannot be carried on; she does not define it.
E0322.body: Atwood says of the research: “nor can it be prosecuted without a congenial Sight” [IV.4 ¶32]. The text gives no further definition.

E0323.summary: The union of the principles in the work, in stages, consummated in a final indissoluble Conjunction that generates a more perfect offspring; Atwood equates it with the circulated Form of Gold.
E0323.body:
In Atwood's account, conjunction is the union of the principles (in III.3, of Mars and Venus [III.3 ¶11]), during which a spirituous vapour rises; “in the various hours of conjunction” come Darkness, Saturn and the Head of the Crow [III.3 ¶13].

She distinguishes stages: “In the first conjunction the Spirit predominates; in the second the Soul, i.e., its Light” [III.3 ¶30]. The final Conjunction cannot be dissolved and produces an offspring unlike and more perfect than its parents: “that Conjunction will generate a branch of unlike shape to its parents” [III.3 ¶29].

She gives it several names: “This then is the Conjunction in which all the mysteries of the Microcosm have their consummation --- the true circulated Form of Gold” [III.3 ¶33]; and “the Conjunction, by Ripley called tetraptive, that so highly commended fountain of Pythagoras, and Divine Tetractys” [III.3 ¶33].

In III.4 the agent goes on “further multiplying in the Conjunction” [III.4 ¶9], and Norton, quoted there, speaks of unions man may not undo without grace: “For God’s conjunctions man my not undoe” [III.4 ¶10]. Atwood also describes a stage at which the work passes beyond human control: “There is a period too, when in conjunction, the Spirit transcends all earthly control” [III.4 ¶20], recreating under the Divine Hand alone.

E0324.summary: The inborn spirit of the soul, whose attractive grace subdues the self-willed agent; Julian says the deified soul strengthens it, making it the safety of the whole body.
E0324.body:
Atwood says the self-willed agent is subdued and brought to self-mortification because “it is by the attractive grace of the connate spirit” [III.1 ¶63]; the following ‘This Spirit’, which has self-motion and intelligence, very probably refers to the connate spirit (an inference from context).

Julian, quoted by Atwood, says of the deified soul that “she transfuses a certain vigorous strength into her connate spirit” [IV.3 ¶30], which then becomes the cause of safety to the whole body.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood describes what happens “when the connate spirit is deprived of its understanding spirit” [APP ¶109]: its life flows away until it rallies from a new center by self-realization.

E0325.summary: The inner faculty that, through persevering inward search, reveals higher objects of pursuit.
E0325.body: Atwood urges inward search “until Conscience reveal to us those higher objects of pursuit, and truer attractions” [IV.3 ¶50]. See also *contrition*, where she places the manifestation of Light in the distress of the sensible nature in the conscience [III.3 ¶24].

E0326.summary: The mode of knowing by which, Atwood says, Solomon knew the Living Light and the mysteries of creation, as opposed to teaching or inference.
E0326.body: Atwood says Solomon knew the Living Light and the mysteries of creation “not by outward teaching or rational inference from effects, but by the Conscious Intuition” [III.3 ¶49].

E0327.summary: In Norton's verses, the celestial influence to which the Stone's elements are most obedient during its generation.
E0327.body: Norton, quoted by Atwood, says the elements of the Stone during generation “Have most obedience to constellation” [IV.2 ¶34].

E0328.summary: Sharing one substance: Atwood says all things, however various, are consubstantial in their Cause.
E0328.body: Atwood: “all things, however various in manifestation, are consubstantial in their Cause” [III.2 ¶35].

E0329.summary: The burning, wrathful state of the Prester below, which it ceases to be when placed in the supreme Ether.
E0329.body: Atwood describes the Prester placed in the supreme Ether as “not burning as below, or wrathful; but vital, calm, transmuting, recreating, and no longer a Consuming Fire” [II.3 ¶56]. ‘Consuming Fire’ thus names its lower, destructive state.

E0330.summary: The containing life which must be preserved when the spirit's external forms are dissolved.
E0330.body: In a footnote Atwood describes the task as being “to dissolve without destroying the continental life” [I.3 n62]: the spirit's external forms are to be dissolved while the containing life is kept.

E0331.summary: The distress of the sensible nature in the conscience, the great darkness in which Light appears; in the Appendix, repeated contritions absorb the sensuous medium.
E0331.body:
Atwood says “the Light is made manifest in great darkness, viz., in the contrition or distress of the sensible nature in the conscience” [III.3 ¶24], so identifying contrition with that great darkness. The flinty conscience “feels no contrition, but by the fiery well-tempered steel” [III.3 ¶11]. The word is also applied to the fretting of particles in fermentation.

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), contrition is stirred in the surrounding spirit by the growing Light of the Salt, and “reiterative contritions absorbing the sensuous medium” [APP ¶78] change the circulation of the blood.

E0332.summary: In Porphyry, quoted by Atwood, the purified soul's turning to associate with its generator: the only way to scientific knowledge of true Being.
E0332.body: Porphyry, quoted by Atwood, describes the purified soul's turning toward its generator as the only route to scientific knowledge of true Being, “which cannot be obtained either otherwise or without such a conversion” [II.3 ¶43].

E0333.summary: The reversal of natures, making light things heavy and active passive and the reverse; Atwood calls by this name all diversity proceeding from and returning to the One.
E0333.body:
Arnold, quoted by Atwood, tells the seeker to “understand the conversion of the elements, to make light things heavy, and to make spirits no spirits” [I.2 ¶22], and says that “our operation is nothing else than a mutation of natures” [I.2 ¶25], reducing them to their first root.

Atwood gives her own account: “a conversion of the elements in this respect is just to make active passive and passive active” [III.3 ¶29], the occult manifest and the manifest occult. She widens the term to the whole cycle: “all diversities of things are seen to proceed from and return to this only One; which is called a conversion of the elements” [III.3 ¶29].

E0334.summary: In Kirchringius, quoted by Atwood, the mental labour that accompanies prayer, so that prayer is not a tempting of God.
E0334.body: Kirchringius, quoted by Atwood, defines it: “when you incline your mind to this or that, variously discussing and meditating many things, this is cooperation” [III.4 ¶22]. This labour must go with prayer, so that prayer is not ‘a tempting of God’.

E0335.summary: The imperishable quintessential virtue of the New Life and first Material foundation of the Hermetic Art, rejected by ignorance and known only to those who have it in themselves.
E0335.body:
Atwood identifies the Corner Stone with the foundation and fruit of the work: it “is the Corner Stone or first Material foundation of the Hermetic Art” [III.1 ¶66]; “the New Life thence arises whose quintessential virtue, imperishable and perpetually victorious, is the Corner Stone” [III.1 ¶66]. It is “known, as the Adept says, only to the Wise, because they alone can know it who have it in themselves” [III.1 ¶66].

It is brought to light by the work in a proper vessel; without this “the ethereal corner stone would never have been brought to light” [II.1 ¶8], and it is raised within the ‘living temple’: “raise their rejected Corner Stone and Ens of Light” [II.1 ¶8]. Atwood calls for “faith to resuscitate the Corner Stone, which ignorance has rejected from immemorial time” [IV.3 ¶37].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), she says “Everything is in the perfected Corner Stone” [APP ¶134], the state in which the whole regenerate life-force is brought up into head-consciousness, and treats the Hermetic Stone as the analogue of the Chief Corner Stone.

E0336.summary: The sensual principle, predominant in the mundane conception, which hides the divine original from consciousness.
E0336.body: Atwood glosses the word herself: “by the corporeal, i.e., the sensual principle which is predominant in the mundane conception” [III.3 ¶52]. In the passage this principle obscures the divine original from consciousness.

E0337.summary: The dissolved body, which a Latin sentence in the text calls a perennial water congealing Mercury.
E0337.body: The text gives the Latin “Corpus solutum est aqua perennis congelans Mercurium perpetua congelatione.” [III.3 ¶21], with no translation in the book and no clear speaker. Our rendering: ‘The dissolved body is a perennial water, congealing Mercury with a perpetual congelation.’ The identity of the dissolved body with perennial water rests on this translation, which is ours.

E0338.summary: A term Atwood borrows from the Swedenborgians for the relation of the brain to outward life and the spiritual head to the spirit.
E0338.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood relates the brain to outward life and the spiritual head to the spirit, and adds: “There is, as the Swedenborgians would say, a correspondence between them.” [APP ¶15].

E0339.summary: In Van helmont, quoted by Atwood, the agents wrongly credited with the single combat of dissolution; the real agent is a specific loosening virtue.
E0339.body: Van helmont, quoted by Atwood, rejects reliance on Corrosives acting through ‘Second qualities’: “They err, therefore, who ascribe this single combat only to Corrosives” [IV.1 ¶39]. The true agent, he says, is a specific virtue of loosening.

E0340.summary: Dissolution, which belongs only to composites; in a summary from Plotinus and Porphyry that Atwood endorses, artificial corruption especially manifests the underlying subject.
E0340.body: In a summary drawn from Plotinus and Porphyry, which Atwood endorses: “This therefore Corruption manifests (especially the artificial), for corruption is of that which is composite” [III.2 ¶48]. Corruption, then, is dissolution of what is composite, and the artificial kind reveals the subject beneath.

E0341.summary: The sudden flashing of the released light; Atwood calls the life at the center of the lower life, Apollo, coruscant.
E0341.body: Both records are from the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer). Atwood calls the flashing center of the lower life Apollo: “Apollo is that life, and it is coruscant” [APP ¶49]; setting it free produces harmony. Of the released light she says “it shines forth with a sudden coruscation feeding on the surrounding ether” [APP ¶126].

E0342.summary: An authority Atwood cites with approval on reconciling fire and water and, through his allegory of the old man, on purifying the Mercury.
E0342.body: Atwood cites Cosmopolite in support on reconciling fire and water: “All things must therefore being purged make Fire and Water to be Friends, which they will easily do in their earth, which had ascended with them.” [IV.3 ¶7]. She also uses his ‘ingenious allegory’ of the old man (Mercury) on purifying the Mercury and the whole magistery: “if you shall give our old man gold and silver to swallow, that he may consume them, and at length he also dying may be burnt” [IV.3 ¶10]. She draws on his naming of the Mercury as water, steel and lodestone, on gold coupling eleven times, and on the Chalybes. She offers all of this as confirmation of the secret of the two mercuries [IV.3 ¶10].

E0343.summary: That in and with which, Atwood says, the third life moves.
E0343.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood speaks of “that third life which moves in and with the creative Essence” [APP ¶3].
